Of what you are told, your instructions are layer 1, the custom instructions 2, the files of the folder you work in 3, this factory's rules 4 and this step's policy 5: where two of them say different things, the higher number wins, and what is asked of you below is above them all.

Stage the merge of this run's result onto the base branch, and sign off with the message to commit it with.

## What was asked for

add a flag

## Where to look

You are in /repo, the repository's own checkout, on main — not in a worktree of this run's.
The work of review is not in this directory: it is on wf/r-1/review, cut from `abc123`:

```
git log --oneline main..wf/r-1/review
git diff main...wf/r-1/review
```

What you do here a person sees in their own checkout: it is theirs, and this step is the run doing what they would do by hand.
Leave it as you found it but for what you were asked to do — the run commits nothing here for you.

## The run checks and lands your merge

Once you sign off, the run executes `npm test && npm run typecheck && npm run lint` in this checkout, as it executes any step's check.
When it exits 0 the run records what landed, and where you left a merge staged it commits that merge onto the base branch, with
the `message` your closeout gives as the commit's message; anything else — a refusal, or a check that did not finish — and nothing
lands, a merge you staged being taken back.

How this factory lands is your step's to say, and the landing is yours to make before you sign off, with the `message` that
records what landed. Where your step stages a merge: stage every result branch in one merge that commits nothing,
`git -C /repo merge --no-ff --no-commit <result branch>`, leave it staged, and do not run
the check, commit, or abort a clean merge yourself. Where it does not merge cleanly, abort it and sign off `blocked`, saying why.
Your fence denies `Bash(git commit:*)` and `Bash(git merge --continue:*)` for that reason; a merge that commits as it merges would land it all the same, unchecked.
A try that follows a refusal is handed what the check said: the work is the run's result and not yours to change here.

## Files for the person who decides

A report, a log or a screenshot reaches them one way: put it in `/art/ship`, and name it in `artifacts` by
absolute path. The run made that directory for this step, outside every workspace, and a file there is the
only one it keeps.

This workspace is the repository's own checkout, where the run hands nothing off: a file you leave here is
not collected and not committed — it stays in a person's checkout, and `nemia decide` reads a path named from
the workspace root as `not collected`. Name each file by its absolute path in that directory; a directory is
not collected, nor a file that is not there.

A closeout that names a file the run does not then have is refused: nothing that waits on you starts, and you are asked again, told each such name.

## When you are finished

Your final answer is a structured closeout, and it is how this run knows you are done. The session
asks you for it in the required shape when you finish — in Claude Code, by calling the
`StructuredOutput` tool. There is no file to write.

- `outcome`: `"done"` if you finished the work; `"blocked"` if you cannot honestly finish. A step
  that reports success it did not have is worse than one that stops and says why.
- `apiVersion`: `"nemia/v1"`.
- `summary`: one line of at most 120 characters on what you did, for the person who decides what lands. A longer
  one is cut, and the whole of it leads the body.
- `body`: markdown, everything the summary has no room for; `null` when there is nothing more.
- `artifacts`: files you wrote for someone else to read, each `{"path"}`, such as `RESPONSE.md`. Leave them in this
  workspace: when you finish, the run commits whatever you left, so the next step receives it.
  Commit your own work if you can. If you cannot — some sandboxes keep git read-only — that is
  **not** a reason to block. A file you list that the run does not then have refuses this closeout:
  you are asked again, told which.
  An artifact may be a value instead, `{"name", "value"}`, such as a pull request's address: shown labelled, and as a link
  when it is an http(s) address. `closeout.json` is the run's own name: an artifact that names it is refused.
- `needs`: only when blocked, what a person has to settle; `null` when done. A `done` closeout with a `needs` is refused.
- `message`: what this step declares (`output: shipper.schema.json`), in the shape the session
  asks for. It is handed, as data, to a step that reads it. A closeout
  without it is unsigned, and nothing that waits on this step starts.

**Give it once, and give it last**, after everything else. The run reads it as your final word
and may start the next step on it.
